rows.label: Concept
rows.text: In a vertical circle gravity's radial pull changes with position, so tension varies: $T_{bottom} = mv_B^2/r + mg$ (maximum) and $T_{top} = mv_T^2/r - mg$ (minimum). A string can only pull, so the loop completes only if $T_{top} \ge 0$, giving the minimum top speed $v_T = \sqrt{gr}$ — for r = 1 m that is 3.13 m/s (NEB 2024).…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text: - T_top = mv_T²/r − mg; T_bottom = mv_B²/r + mg - v_T,min = √(gr); v_B,min = √(5gr) - Energy: ½mv_B² = ½mv_T² + 2mgr

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: **Energy Conservation (No Non-Conservative Work):** Total mechanical energy ($K + U$) is conserved if only gravity and tension act (tension does zero work). $v^2 = u^2 - 2gh$ where $h = R(1 - \cos heta)$ from the lowest point.  ·  **String vs. Rod Constraint:** - **String:** Can only pull (tension $T \ge 0$). If $T o 0$, the string goes slack and the particle follows a parabolic projectile path until the string tightens again. - **Rigid Rod:** Can push or pull ($T$ can be negative/compressive). The particle completes the circle even if speed at top is zero (but $v_{top} \ge 0$ is required).

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: The factor √(5gr) for minimum bottom speed (string) is the single most tested result in NEB exams.  ·  Always distinguish between string (T ≥ 0) and rod (T can be negative / pushing).

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: **Top vs bottom minimum speeds:** top needs √(gr); bottom needs √(5gr) — five times the energy scale.  ·  **String vs rod:** a string can only pull (v_top ≥ √gr); a rod can push (v_top ≥ 0).

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: Derive v_top(min) = √(gr) from the force equation at the top.  ·  Derive v_bottom(min) = √(5gr) using energy conservation.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: **The taut-string condition:** the loop survives only if $T_{top} \ge 0$, i.e. gravity alone can bend the path at the top.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: $T_{top} = mv_T^2/r - mg$; $T_{bottom} = mv_B^2/r + mg$.  ·  $v_{T,min} = \sqrt{gr}$; $v_{B,min} = \sqrt{5gr}$; $T_{bottom,max} = 6mg$ at the limit.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Water stays in a bucket swung overhead for the same reason: at √(gr) the water presses on the bucket bottom, not the other way.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — The Circle That Fights Gravity Whirl a bucket of water overhead and nothing spills — provided you spin fast enough. Motion in a vertical circle differs from every previous case because gravity's pull along the radius changes constantly: strongest at the bottom, weakest at the top.…  ·  ## 2. Fundamental Concepts ### 2.1 The changing tension A bob of mass $m$ on a string of length $r$ moves in a vertical circle with speed $v$. Tension must supply centripetal force together with (or against) gravity's radial component: - **At the lowest point:** tension and gravity oppose radially: $T_{bottom} - mg = \dfrac{mv_B^2}{r} \Rightarrow T_{bottom} = \dfrac{mv_B^2}{r}…  ·  ## 3. Conceptual Relationships - **To Topic 24:** $F_c$ here is supplied by tension plus gravity's radial component — the general principle applied. - **To Conservation of energy (Topic 19):** speed differences between top and bottom come purely from the 2r height change.…

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: **Critical Speeds (String):** $v_{top} \ge \sqrt{gR}$ (taut string at top); $v_{bottom} \ge \sqrt{5gR}$ (minimum to complete circle). At the horizontal point ($ heta=90^\circ$), minimum speed is $\sqrt{2gR}$ for the string to remain taut.  ·  If the string goes slack, the body becomes a projectile — follow parabolic path.  ·  T_bottom = 6mg only when v_bottom = √(5gr) — this is the minimum case.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: NEB frequently asks: 'Find the minimum speed at the bottom to complete the vertical circle'.  ·  Verified PYQ: minimum top velocity (2024, 3m).  ·  "At the highest point, gravity itself acts as the centripetal force in the limiting case."
